Bipolar Junction Transistors

Learn how two pn junctions form a controllable current source, how junction bias determines cutoff, forward-active, and saturation, and how to establish reliable DC operating points.

Begin here · no prior BJT knowledge assumed

What problem does a transistor solve?

A transistor lets a relatively small input action control a larger output current. In a BJT, the decisive physical variable is the base-emitter voltage, which controls carrier injection. Circuit analysis often also uses base current because it is easy to measure and connect to a bias network.

Amplifier role

A small change in \(v_{BE}\) creates a much larger proportional change in collector current.

Switch role

Cutoff approximates an open switch; saturation approximates a closed switch with small \(v_{CE}\).

Bias role

DC networks establish a stable operating point before a time-varying signal is applied.

Essential terminal quantities

QuantityDefinitionMeaning for an npn
\(v_{BE}=v_B-v_E\)Base-emitter voltageControls emitter injection; forward bias is usually around \(0.6\)-\(0.8\ \mathrm{V}\) in simple silicon models.
\(v_{BC}=v_B-v_C\)Base-collector voltageIts sign distinguishes forward-active from saturation.
\(v_{CE}=v_C-v_E\)Collector-emitter voltageOutput voltage and switch headroom.
\(i_B,i_C,i_E\)Base, collector, and emitter currentsThey satisfy \(i_E=i_C+i_B\).

Important terminology

“Bipolar” means both electrons and holes participate in the device physics. An npn still has electron transport as its dominant controlled current, while holes participate in base current and junction behavior.

Topic 6.1

BJT Structure and Modes of Operation

Use the two pn-junction viewpoint before memorizing circuit models.

Section introduction

One transistor, three doped regions, and two junctions

An npn consists of an n-type emitter, p-type base, and n-type collector. The regions are deliberately asymmetric: the emitter is heavily doped to inject carriers, the base is thin and lightly doped to minimize recombination, and the collector is designed to collect carriers and withstand voltage.

Expanded beginner lesson

Build the physical picture step by step

Emitter

The heavily doped emitter supplies a large concentration of carriers. In an npn, these are electrons.

Base

The base is intentionally thin. A small fraction of injected electrons recombines and creates base current.

Collector

The collector-base depletion field sweeps most injected electrons into the collector during forward-active operation.

Why two diodes are not enough

Two separate back-to-back diodes lack the shared thin base that permits injected carriers to cross and be collected.

Junction-bias test for an npn

RegionEmitter-base junctionCollector-base junctionCircuit behavior
CutoffNot forward biasedUsually reverse biasedSwitch OFF; \(i_B\approx i_C\approx0\)
Forward-activeForward biasedReverse biasedAmplifier/current-source region
SaturationForward biasedForward biasedSwitch ON; small \(v_{CE}\)
Reverse-activeReverse biasedForward biasedRoles of emitter and collector are reversed; gain is usually poor

Voltage identities that prevent sign mistakes

\[ v_{CE}=v_C-v_E,\qquad v_{BE}=v_B-v_E,\qquad v_{BC}=v_B-v_C \] \[ \boxed{v_{CE}=v_{BE}-v_{BC}} \]

In forward-active operation, \(v_{BE}>0\) while \(v_{BC}<0\). In saturation, both are positive, so \(v_{CE}\) becomes small.

Common beginner error

Do not identify saturation merely from a large collector current. Saturation is a junction-bias condition: both the emitter-base and collector-base junctions are forward biased.

Topic 6.2

Large-Signal Exponential Relations

Connect carrier injection to terminal currents.

Section introduction

The BJT is fundamentally controlled by \(v_{BE}\)

In forward-active operation, collector current is set primarily by the exponential emitter-base injection law. Base current is required because some carriers recombine in the base, but \(\beta\) is not the fundamental control mechanism.

Expanded beginner theory

From the diode law to BJT current gain

Collector-current law

\[ \boxed{i_C\approx I_S e^{v_{BE}/V_T}}, \qquad \boxed{V_T=\frac{kT}{q}} \]

At room temperature, \(V_T\approx25.9\ \mathrm{mV}\). Increasing \(v_{BE}\) by \(V_T\ln 10\approx59.6\ \mathrm{mV}\) increases ideal collector current by a factor of ten.

Current continuity

\[i_E=i_C+i_B\]

The emitter supplies the current that exits through both collector and base terminals.

Common-emitter gain

\[\beta=\frac{i_C}{i_B}\]

For a specified collector current, \(i_B=i_C/\beta\).

Common-base gain

\[\alpha=\frac{i_C}{i_E}\]

\(\alpha\) is close to one because most emitter-injected carriers reach the collector.

Gain conversion

\[ \alpha=\frac{\beta}{\beta+1}, \qquad \beta=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha} \]

Why \(0.7\ \mathrm{V}\) is only an approximation

There is no abrupt threshold at \(0.7\ \mathrm{V}\). The exponential curve is continuous. The value \(0.7\ \mathrm{V}\) is a convenient constant-drop approximation over a common current range.

Topic 6.3

Output Characteristics and Early Effect

Read the common-emitter curve family as a map of operating behavior.

Section introduction

Why collector current is almost—but not perfectly—independent of \(v_{CE}\)

In forward-active operation, the collector-base junction sweeps injected carriers into the collector. Ideally, \(i_C\) would depend only on \(v_{BE}\) or \(i_B\). Real curves tilt upward because increasing collector-base reverse bias narrows the neutral base.

Expanded beginner theory

How to read a family of BJT output curves

Select a base-current curve. Each curve corresponds to one fixed \(i_B\) or approximately one fixed \(v_{BE}\).
Locate the knee. At very small \(v_{CE}\), the transistor is saturated and current depends strongly on \(v_{CE}\).
Move into forward-active. Beyond the knee, current becomes approximately \(\beta i_B\).
Observe the slight slope. The upward tilt represents Early effect and finite output resistance.

First-order active model

\[i_C\approx\beta i_B\]

Early-effect model

\[ i_C\approx I_S e^{v_{BE}/V_T}\left(1+\frac{v_{CE}}{V_A}\right) \]

Output resistance

\[r_o\approx\frac{V_A}{I_C}\]

Engineering meaning

Larger \(V_A\) gives flatter curves, larger \(r_o\), and more ideal current-source behavior.

Distinguish BJT saturation from curve clipping

BJT saturation occurs at low \(v_{CE}\), near the left knee. It is unrelated to a plot reaching its upper current limit. The simulator terminates any off-scale curve cleanly instead of drawing a false flat top.

Topic 6.4 · Example 1

Two-Supply BJT DC Bias

Assume, solve, and verify—then change the model if verification fails.

Section introduction

DC bias analysis is a consistency problem

A transistor equation is valid only in its intended operating region. Start with a plausible region, solve the circuit, and check the resulting junction biases. If the result violates the assumptions, repeat with a different model.

Step-by-step solving framework

Forward-active test followed by saturation solution

Assume forward-active and use \(V_{BE}\approx0.7\ \mathrm{V}\), \(I_C=\beta I_B\), and \(I_E=(\beta+1)I_B\).
Solve the base-emitter loop: \[ I_B=\frac{V_{BB}-V_{BE}}{R_{BB}+(\beta+1)R_E}. \]
Compute \(V_E\), \(V_B\), \(V_C\), and \(V_{CE}\). Check whether \(V_C>V_B\), so the collector-base junction is reverse biased.
If active verification fails, solve saturation using \(V_{BE(sat)}\) and \(V_{CE(sat)}\), together with \(I_E=I_C+I_B\).

Saturation equation in one unknown

Let \(V_E\) be the unknown. Then

\[ \frac{V_E}{R_E} = \frac{V_{CC}-(V_E+V_{CE(sat)})}{R_C} + \frac{V_{BB}-(V_E+V_{BE(sat)})}{R_{BB}}. \]

After finding \(V_E\), calculate every current and verify KCL.

Topic 6.4 · Example 2

Voltage-Divider Bias with Emitter Feedback

Reduce the divider to a Thevenin source and solve the base loop.

Section introduction

Why emitter resistance stabilizes the operating point

If current rises, the emitter voltage rises. That reduces \(v_{BE}=v_B-v_E\), opposing the original increase. This negative feedback makes the bias less sensitive to transistor \(\beta\).

Expanded beginner derivation

Thevenin reduction and base-current solution

Divider equivalent

\[ V_{TH}=V_{CC}\frac{R_{B2}}{R_{B1}+R_{B2}}, \qquad R_{TH}=R_{B1}\parallel R_{B2} \]

Active-region base current

\[ I_B=\frac{V_{TH}-V_{BE}}{R_{TH}+(\beta+1)R_E} \]
Find \(V_{TH}\) and \(R_{TH}\) while treating the base as the load connected to the divider.
Calculate \(I_B\), then \(I_C=\beta I_B\) and \(I_E=(\beta+1)I_B\).
Find \(V_E=I_E R_E\), \(V_B=V_E+V_{BE}\), and \(V_C=V_{CC}-I_C R_C\).
Verify \(V_C>V_B\) and \(V_{CE}\) is safely above saturation.

Stiff-divider approximation

If divider current is much larger than base current, \(V_B\approx V_{TH}\). The exact Thevenin method remains safer and automatically includes base loading.

Topic 6.4 · Example 3

Complementary Push-Pull Emitter Follower

Use polarity to decide which transistor conducts.

Section introduction

One transistor sources current; the other sinks current

Complementary emitter followers use an npn for positive output current and a pnp for negative output current. Around zero input, neither transistor may conduct in a simple unbiased stage, producing a crossover dead zone.

Expanded beginner analysis

Piecewise reasoning for a complementary pair

Positive drive

The npn turns on when the base is about \(0.7\ \mathrm{V}\) above the output. The pnp is off.

Near zero

If \(|v_B-v_O|<0.7\ \mathrm{V}\), both devices can be off and the load returns the output toward ground.

Negative drive

The pnp turns on when its base is about \(0.7\ \mathrm{V}\) below the output. The npn is off.

Base-current loading through the drive resistor

For positive operation with the npn on,

\[ \frac{V_{\text{drive}}-(V_O+V_{BE})}{R_B} = \frac{V_O}{R_L(\beta+1)}. \]

The output is slightly lower than the ideal \(V_{\text{drive}}-V_{BE}\) because base current creates an additional drop across \(R_B\).

Crossover distortion

A real class-B output stage has a dead zone near zero. Practical class-AB stages add a bias network that keeps both devices slightly conducting and reduces crossover distortion.
